mainTopic: שהחיינו on new purchases, blessings on good and bad news, vain prayers and trust in ה׳, and prayers for times of danger
overview: This amud opens by finishing the debate between רב הונא and רבי יוחנן about when a person says שהחיינו on a new purchase. It gives two versions of their argument. A ברייתא with רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה seems to leave רבי יוחנן without a תנא in the second version, and the גמרא defends him using the rule כח דהתירא עדיף. The גמרא then explains the משנה's lines about blessing on bad and good news: a ברכה follows what is happening now, not how things may turn out. Next it discusses why praying for a baby's gender is a תפילת שוא, answering a challenge from לאה and דינה in two ways. Stories about הלל and other sages teach that a person should trust in ה׳ rather than fear bad news. The proper fear is fear about תורה. The amud ends with prayers for entering and leaving a city, a bathhouse, and bloodletting, along with אביי's objections to some of the wording.

steps.title: What everyone agrees on in the first version
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws an inference from the first version. If someone bought an item and then bought the same kind again, everyone agrees no שהחיינו is said.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn from this that if he bought something and then bought another one like it, everyone agrees he does not need to make a ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing out the first version of the dispute by pointing out a case where רב הונא and רבי יוחנן do not argue at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the argument was about a person who already owns an item and buys a new one. The case of buying, then buying again, is a stronger case for no ברכה, because he already said שהחיינו when he bought the first one. So even רבי יוחנן, who requires a ברכה in the 'already owns' case, agrees that no ברכה is said here.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference; we can learn from this
He bought, and then bought again
He must make a ברכה (here: שהחיינו)

steps.confusionAlert: There are two different cases here. 'יש לו וקנה' means he already owns one and buys another, without having made a ברכה on the first. 'קנה וחזר וקנה' means he bought one, presumably made a ברכה, and then bought again. Keep these two cases separate, because the whole sugya depends on the difference.

phrases.english: This implies that when he bought and then bought again,
everyone agrees he need not recite a blessing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the first version of the dispute, which began earlier
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In the first version, buying and then buying again requires no שהחיינו according to everyone.

steps.title: Second version of the dispute between רב הונא and רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, רב הונא says that buying and then buying again requires no ברכה. רבי יוחנן says that even in that case a ברכה is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say it this way. רב הונא said: the rule of making a ברכה was only taught when he had not bought this before and now buys it. But if he bought it before and buys again, he does not need a ברכה. רבי יוחנן said: even if he bought it before and buys again, he must make a ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives an alternate version of the same argument. Here the dispute is moved to a different case: buying again after having already bought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, they argued about 'already owns one.' In this version, they argue about 'bought and bought again.' This makes רבי יוחנן very far-reaching: he requires שהחיינו even after a ברכה was already said on the same kind of item.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say; introduces a second version
They only taught this rule in the case of

phrases.english: And some say:
Rav Huna said:
They only taught this
where he had not bought before and then bought,
but if he bought and then bought again —
he need not recite a blessing.
And Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Even if he bought and then bought again —
he must recite a blessing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a competing version of the dispute that was just concluded
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא: buying, then buying again, requires no ברכה. רבי יוחנן: even then, a ברכה is required.

steps.title: What everyone agrees on in the second version
steps.stepSummary: From the second version, we infer that someone who already owns an item and buys another one must say שהחיינו according to everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn from this that if he already has one and buys another, everyone agrees he must make a ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out the case where both sides agree in the second version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רב הונא only exempts the case of 'bought and bought again,' he must agree that 'already owns one, but never made a ברכה' still needs a ברכה. So in this version, nobody exempts the 'יש לו' case. This detail will cause the problem in step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: He already has one, and buys another

phrases.english: This implies that when he already has one and buys —
everyone agrees he must recite a blessing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the agreed-upon case out of the second version
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In the second version, 'already owns one' requires שהחיינו according to everyone.

steps.title: A ברייתא: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה on owning a similar item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. רבי מאיר says that if you already own a similar item, you do not say a ברכה. רבי יהודה says you say a ברכה either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: If someone built a new house and has no other house like it, or bought new vessels and has none like them, he must make a ברכה. If he does have similar ones, he does not need a ברכה. These are the words of רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: either way, he must make a ברכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to set up a challenge. The actual problem is spelled out in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא argues about the 'already owns a similar one' case. רבי מאיר exempts it, and רבי יהודה requires a ברכה. The ברייתא never mentions 'bought, then bought again,' so at first it looks like neither תנא requires a ברכה there. That assumption will matter for רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged; introduces a challenge from a ברייתא
One like it; a similar item

phrases.english: They raised an objection: One who built a new house
and does not have one like it,
or bought new vessels
and does not have ones like them —
must recite a blessing.
If he has ones like them —

phrases.aramaic: אֵין צָרִיךְ לְבָרֵךְ, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר.
phrases.english: he need not recite a blessing; these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין כָּךְ וּבֵין כָּךְ צָרִיךְ לְבָרֵךְ.
phrases.english: Either way, he must recite a blessing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an outside source to test the second version
steps.kashyaTarget: The second version of רבי יוחנן's view
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא only argues about 'already owns a similar one.' It leaves no room for requiring a ברכה after buying again.

steps.title: In the second version, רבי יוחנן matches no תנא
steps.stepSummary: The first version fits the ברייתא neatly. In the second version, רב הונא fits רבי יהודה, but רבי יוחנן fits neither רבי מאיר nor רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for the first version: רב הונא follows רבי מאיר, and רבי יוחנן follows רבי יהודה. But for the second version: fine, רב הונא follows רבי יהודה. But whose view does רבי יוחנן follow? He follows neither רבי מאיר nor רבי יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states its challenge. In the second version, רבי יוחנן's opinion has no support from either תנא in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the dispute is about 'owns one,' which lines up exactly with רבי מאיר against רבי יהודה. In the second version, everyone requires a ברכה for 'owns one,' which is רבי יהודה's view. But רבי יוחנן goes further and requires a ברכה even after buying again. רבי מאיר clearly does not hold this, and even רבי יהודה only requires a ברכה in the 'owns one' case.
steps.whatToRemember: First version: רב הונא = רבי מאיר, and רבי יוחנן = רבי יהודה. Second version: רב הונא = רבי יהודה, and רבי יוחנן matches no one. This is a strong challenge to the second version.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה's 'either way' explicitly covers only whether he owns a similar item or not. The question assumes it does not cover buying again after already making a ברכה, which is why רבי יוחנן seems to go beyond רבי יהודה too. The next step rejects this assumption.

phrases.english: Granted, according to the first version —
Rav Huna follows Rabbi Meir,
and Rabbi Yoḥanan follows Rabbi Yehuda.
But according to the latter version,
granted, Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yehuda,
but Rabbi Yoḥanan, whose view did he state?
Not like Rabbi Meir
and not like Rabbi Yehuda!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the challenge set up by the ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן in the לישנא בתרא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An אמורא should hold like some תנא. In the second version, רבי יוחנן requires a ברכה after buying again, which neither רבי מאיר nor רבי יהודה supports.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן actually follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן holds like רבי יהודה, who also requires a ברכה when one bought and then bought again. The ברייתא chose the case of 'already owns and buys' only to show how far רבי מאיר goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן could tell you: according to רבי יהודה, even if you bought and then bought again, you also have to say a ברכה. The reason the ברייתא sets their argument in the case of 'he already owns one and buys' is to show you how far רבי מאיר goes. Even when he buys while already owning one, רבי מאיר says no ברכה is needed. So all the more so, if he bought and then bought again, no ברכה is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן from the problem in Step 5. It shows that he really matches רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא never said what רבי יהודה holds about 'bought and bought again', so רבי יוחנן can say רבי יהודה requires a ברכה there too. The case of 'already owns and buys' is where a ברכה seems most needed. רבי מאיר says no ברכה even there, which teaches that he certainly says no ברכה in the weaker case.

keyTerms.meaning: To show you the strength (how far-reaching) of someone's opinion
He already owns one and buys another
He bought one and then bought again

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume a מחלוקת covers only the case it mentions. Often a ברייתא picks the most extreme case on purpose to show how far one side goes, and the other cases follow automatically.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan could say to you:
The same is true according to Rabbi Yehuda:
if he bought and then bought again
he also must say a blessing.
And the fact that they argue
about one who already owns and buys
is to show you how far Rabbi Meir goes:
that even if he buys while already owning one
he does not need to say a blessing,
and all the more so if he bought and then bought again
that he does not need to say a blessing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 5 against רבי יוחנן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the ברייתא: the case chosen shows how far one side goes, not the whole scope of the argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the ברייתא only mentions 'already owns and buys', רבי יהודה might not require a ברכה for 'bought and bought again', leaving רבי יוחנן with no תנא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יהודה requires a ברכה in both cases, so רבי יוחנן follows רבי יהודה.

steps.title: Why not show how far רבי יהודה goes instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the goal was to show how far one side goes, the ברייתא could have set the argument in the case of 'bought and bought again'. That case would show how far רבי יהודה goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: So let them argue about the case of bought and then bought again, where according to רבי מאיר no ברכה is needed. That would show you how far רבי יהודה goes!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer just given. It asks why the ברייתא chose to highlight רבי מאיר's view and not רבי יהודה's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Bought and bought again' is the weakest case for a ברכה. If רבי יהודה requires one even there, that would show his opinion at its strongest. So why did the ברייתא prefer to show רבי מאיר's strength?

keyTerms.meaning: So let them argue (about a different case)

phrases.english: So let them argue about one who bought and then bought again,
where (according to Rabbi Meir) he does not need to say a blessing,
to show you how far Rabbi Yehuda goes!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning of the תירוץ in Step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא chose its case to show רבי מאיר's strength
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא could just as well have chosen the other case to show רבי יהודה's strength. So why favor רבי מאיר?

steps.title: Showing a lenient view is preferred
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא prefers to show how far the lenient view goes. Here that is רבי מאיר, who does not require a ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Showing the strength of a lenient view is more preferable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 7 in one short line. A ברייתא prefers to highlight the lenient side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Anyone can be strict just to be safe, so a strict view does not prove much. Being lenient shows that the תנא is confident in his ruling, so that is the more important thing to show. Here, 'lenient' means not requiring a ברכה, which is רבי מאיר's view.

keyTerms.meaning: The strength of a lenient (permitting) position

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן follows רבי יהודה. The ברייתא's choice of case is explained by the rule כח דהתירא עדיף: showing how far a lenient view goes is preferred.
steps.whyThisMatters: כח דהתירא עדיף is a principle that comes up across ש״ס. It explains why a משנה or ברייתא often frames an argument to show how far the lenient side goes.

phrases.english: Showing the strength of a lenient view is preferable to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: General principle of how texts are framed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sides' strength would be equally worth showing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Showing the lenient side's strength is preferred, so the ברייתא highlights רבי מאיר.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: blessing on bad news
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: one says a ברכה on bad things.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one says a ברכה on the bad, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic by quoting the next line of the משנה. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches that one blesses based on what is happening now. If something is bad now, one says the ברכה for bad news, even if it may turn out good later.

keyTerms.meaning: He blesses on the bad (says the ברכה for bad news)
Etc. (short for the rest of the quote)

phrases.english: One says a blessing on the bad, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the שהחיינו discussion and starts a new section of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One says a ברכה on something bad based on how it is now, even if it may become good.

steps.title: What case is the משנה talking about
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a real example of something bad now that turns out good later.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what real-life situation the משנה means. This prepares the example that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's rule is abstract. The גמרא wants a concrete case where something is bad now but good in the end.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? / What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: What is the case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for an example of the משנה just quoted
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete case of something bad now that will later be good

steps.title: A flooded field: good later, bad now
steps.stepSummary: Example: a dam bursts and floods a man's field. Later the silt will improve his soil, but right now it is bad, so he says the ברכה for bad news.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, a dam broke and water flooded his land. In the end this is good for him, because the water leaves silt on the land and makes it better. But right now, at least, it is bad.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question with a clear case: a field flooded by a burst dam.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The flood leaves rich soil, so the field will grow better crops later. But right now his field is under water and ruined. The ברכה follows the present situation, so he says the ברכה for bad news.

keyTerms.meaning: A breach (a break in a dam or riverbank)
Silt / rich soil left by water

steps.whatToRemember: A ברכה follows what is happening now. Bad now means the ברכה for bad news, even if good comes later.

phrases.english: For example, when a dam broke and flooded his land,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּטָבָא הִיא לְדִידֵיהּ,
phrases.english: even though it is good for him,
because the land gets covered with silt and improves,
right now, at least, it is bad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of Step 10
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A burst dam floods a field. It will improve the soil later but is bad now.

steps.title: The משנה's next line: a ברכה on good things
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: one says a ברכה on good things.
steps.simpleTranslation: And on the good, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה so it can explain it. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the משנה ruled that you bless based on how things look now, even if a bad thing will turn good later. This line gives the reverse case: something good now that may become bad later. The rule is the same: you go by the present.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc. — the rest of the quote

phrases.english: And on the good, etc.
phrases.notes: Short for the full line: one blesses on the good that may later turn bad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the 'bad turning good' case to its mirror image, 'good turning bad'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One blesses on something good now, even if it may turn bad later.

steps.title: Asking for a real example
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the משנה means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a concrete example of something good now that could turn bad later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors Step 10, where the גמרא asked the same question about the bad case. The question is a request for a clear picture, not an attack.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it look like? / What is the case?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for an example of the line just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real-life case of something good now that may later be bad.

steps.title: Example: finding a lost object
steps.stepSummary: A man finds a valuable lost object. If the king hears about it he will take it, but right now it is good.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, a man finds a lost object. It might turn out badly for him, because if the king hears about it he will take it away. Still, right now it is good.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with an example: finding a lost object. It is good now, even though the king might take it away later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In those times, the king's law could claim found objects. So the find might end up bringing the man loss or trouble. Even so, he says the ברכה for good news, because we judge by the present moment.
steps.whatToRemember: For ברכות on news, you go by how it is right now, not by how it may end up: bad-now-good-later gets the bad ברכה, and good-now-bad-later gets the good ברכה.

phrases.english: For example, where he found a lost object,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּרָעָה הִיא לְדִידֵיהּ,
phrases.english: even though it is bad for him,
since if the king heard about it,
he would take it from him,
right now, at least, it is good.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by giving a concrete case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Finding a lost object: good now, but it may be taken away by the king later.

steps.title: Praying for a baby's gender is a vain prayer
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a husband who prays that his pregnant wife will have a boy is making a תפילת שוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his wife was pregnant and he said, 'May it be God's will that she gives birth to a boy,' this is a vain prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line of the משנה. Praying to decide the gender of a baby already formed is a תפילת שוא, a prayer said for nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the baby's gender is already set, so asking to change it is like asking to undo the past. This ruling is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: A vain prayer, one that cannot help

phrases.english: If his wife was pregnant
and he said: 'May it be [God's] will that she give birth [to a male], etc.' —
this is a vain prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic from the משנה: prayers that cannot work.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Praying to change the gender of a baby already conceived is a תפילת שוא.

steps.title: Does prayer really not help? רב יוסף cites the birth of דינה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether prayer truly does not help, and רב יוסף challenges the משנה from the verse about דינה's birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does prayer really not help? רב יוסף objects from the verse: 'And afterwards she gave birth to a daughter, and called her name דינה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the משנה: is it really true that prayer cannot help here? רב יוסף brings a verse about לאה to challenge it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said praying about the gender is useless. רב יוסף points to the verse about דינה's birth, which will be explained to show a gender changing during pregnancy. If that happened, prayer can affect the gender.

phrases.english: And does prayer not help?
Rav Yosef raises an objection:
'And afterwards she bore a daughter
and called her name Dinah':

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא מַהֲנֵי רַחֲמֵי? מֵתִיב רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's ruling just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's claim that praying about a baby's gender is useless.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verse, as explained by רב, shows that a baby's gender changed during pregnancy. So prayer can make a difference.

steps.title: רב's reading: לאה's judgment changed the baby to a girl
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that 'afterwards' means after לאה judged that another son would leave רחל with fewer tribes than the maidservants, and the baby immediately became a girl.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'afterwards' mean? רב said: After לאה made a judgment about herself. She said: Twelve tribes will come from יעקב. Six came from me and four from the maidservants, which makes ten. If this baby is a boy, my sister רחל will not even be like one of the maidservants. Right away the baby turned into a girl, as it says: 'and she called her name דינה.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the proof behind רב יוסף's objection. רב explains the extra word 'afterwards' to mean that לאה's baby changed from a boy into a girl.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לאה worked out that if she had a seventh son, רחל could have only one tribe, fewer than each maidservant had. Because of her concern for her sister, the baby became a girl, named דינה after לאה's 'judgment' (דין). This seems to prove that a fetus's gender can still change, so prayer about it is not useless.

keyTerms.meaning: Made a judgment / reasoned it out

steps.confusionAlert: The name דינה is a wordplay on דין, 'judgment.' The proof comes from the extra word 'afterwards' together with the name, not from the plain story.

phrases.english: What is meant by 'afterwards'?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: לְאַחַר שֶׁדָּנָה לֵאָה דִּין בְּעַצְמָהּ
phrases.english: Rav said: After Leah passed judgment on herself
and said: Twelve tribes
are destined to come from Jacob;
six came from me
and four from the maidservants — that is ten.
If this one is male,
my sister Rachel will not even be
like one of the maidservants.
Immediately it was turned into a daughter,
as it is said: 'And she called her name Dinah.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the content of רב יוסף's objection by explaining the verse.
steps.raayaObject: That a fetus's gender can change, so praying about it is not useless.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The verse about דינה's birth, as explained by רב.

steps.title: Miracles are no proof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: we do not bring proofs from miracles.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not cite miracles [as proof].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב יוסף's proof. What happened with לאה was a miracle, and ordinary הלכה is not learned from miracles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא accepts that the baby changed for לאה, but calls it a נס. A normal person cannot pray expecting a miracle, so for him the prayer is still a תפילת שוא. The משנה's ruling stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה stands: praying to change a fetus's gender is a תפילת שוא. לאה's case was a miracle, and miracles do not set ordinary הלכה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a general rule across ש״ס: a miraculous event cannot serve as a source for normal practical law.

phrases.english: One does not cite miraculous events.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Steps 16 and 17.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof from לאה, without denying that the story happened.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof relies on a miracle, and miracles cannot be used to derive normal הלכה.

steps.title: Second answer: לאה's prayer was within the first forty days
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another way to answer רב יוסף's challenge. לאה prayed within forty days of conception, when the gender was not yet fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: the story of לאה happened within the first forty days of the pregnancy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer to the question from דינה's birth. It says לאה's prayer came early in the pregnancy, so it does not contradict the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer said דינה's birth was a miracle, and we do not learn from miracles. This answer says no miracle was needed: in the first forty days the gender is not yet set, so prayer can really work. The משנה's תפילת שוא only applies after forty days, once the gender is fixed.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces a second, alternative answer
The incident of לאה, her prayer about the baby
Forty days, the point after which the baby's gender is fixed

steps.confusionAlert: This does not replace the first answer, that we do not learn from miracles. It is a second, separate answer. Either one is enough to defend the משנה.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
the incident of Leah
was within forty days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, non-miracle answer to the challenge from דינה, alongside step 18's 'we do not learn from miracles'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Time limit: the case happened during a stage when prayer can still change the outcome
steps.terutzHavaAmina: לאה's prayer changed a fixed gender, which would show the משנה is wrong
steps.terutzMaskana: לאה prayed within forty days, before the gender was fixed, so her prayer was not a תפילת שוא

steps.title: A ברייתא on what to pray for at each stage of pregnancy
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists the right prayer for each stage of pregnancy. From day three to day forty one prays for a boy, which supports the forty-day answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: During the first three days, a person should pray that the seed not spoil. From day three until day forty, he should pray that the baby will be a boy. From day forty until three months, he should pray that it will not be a deformed, flat-fish shape. From three months until six, he should pray that it will not be stillborn. From six months until nine, he should pray that the baby will come out safely.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support the answer it just gave. The ברייתא shows that praying for a boy is allowed, and works, between day three and day forty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each stage of pregnancy has its own proper prayer. Praying for a boy appears only in the window from day three to day forty, which proves that gender can still be affected then. After that, the prayers change to the baby's health and safe birth.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
He should pray; literally, ask for mercy
Will spoil or rot, meaning the seed will fail to start a pregnancy
A deformed fetus shaped like a flat fish

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the משנה's ruling is not against prayer in general. Every stage of pregnancy has a proper prayer, and only a prayer to change something already decided is useless.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
the first three days —
a person should pray that it not putrefy.
From three until forty
he should pray that it will be male.
From forty days until three months —
he should pray that it not be a flat-fish shape.
From three months until six —
he should pray that it not be stillborn.
From six until nine —
he should pray that it emerge safely.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support step 19's forty-day answer.
steps.raayaObject: That praying for a boy can work before day forty
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא listing the proper prayers for each stage of pregnancy

steps.title: Challenge: gender is decided at the moment of conception
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how prayer can help even before forty days. רב יצחק בריה דרב אמי taught that gender is decided at conception by which parent emits seed first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does prayer really help? But רב יצחק, son of רב אמי, said: If the man emits seed first, the woman gives birth to a girl. If the woman emits seed first, she gives birth to a boy, as it says: 'When a woman emits seed and gives birth to a male.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא it just quoted. If gender is set at the moment of conception, then even in the first forty days prayer should not be able to change it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יצחק's teaching means the outcome is fixed from the start, based on which parent emitted seed first. He learns it from the פסוק, which links the woman's emitting seed with the birth of a male. That leaves no window in which prayer can change the gender.

phrases.english: And does prayer help?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַמֵּי:
phrases.english: But didn't Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Ami say:
if the man emits seed first — she bears a female,
if the woman emits seed first — she bears a male.
As it is stated:
"When a woman emits seed and bears a male"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ברייתא of step 20, which says praying for a boy works until day forty.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that one may pray for a boy from day three to day forty
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If gender is fixed at conception by which parent emits seed first, prayer afterward cannot change it.

steps.title: Answer: when both emit seed at the same moment
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a case where both parents emitted seed at the same moment. In that case gender is not fixed, so prayer can decide it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where both of them emitted seed at the same moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the ברייתא to one specific case. When neither parent was first, רב יצחק's rule does not decide the gender, and prayer can.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יצחק's rule only works when one parent is first. If both emitted seed at the same moment, the gender is open, and that is when the ברייתא's prayer for a boy helps. So both teachings are true, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? Introduces a narrowing of the case

steps.whatToRemember: Praying for a boy works only within forty days, and only when the parents emitted seed at the same moment. Otherwise it is a תפילת שוא.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here —
such as where both of them emitted seed at once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Gender is always fixed at conception, so prayer never helps
steps.terutzMaskana: When both parents emit seed at the same moment, the gender is open and prayer can decide it

steps.title: Next line of the משנה: a man walking on the road
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה: a man walking on the road who hears a scream and prays it is not from his house.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'He was coming along the road.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next case in the משנה. This line only sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a man coming along the road hears a scream from the city and prays that it is not from his house. That prayer is a תפילת שוא, because whatever happened has already happened. The גמרא is about to add a story on this theme.

keyTerms.meaning: He was coming along the road (quoting the משנה)

phrases.english: He was coming along the road.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of the pregnant wife and opens the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Praying that a scream already heard is not from one's own house is a תפילת שוא

steps.title: הלל heard a scream and trusted it was not from his house
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells that הלל הזקן heard a scream in the city and said he was certain it was not from his house. The פסוק 'He shall not fear bad news' is applied to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: There was an incident with הלל הזקן, who was coming along the road and heard a scream in the city. He said: I am certain that this is not in my house. About him the פסוק says: 'He shall not fear bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about הלל in the same situation as the משנה. Instead of making a useless prayer, הלל showed calm trust in ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches what not to do: pray to change something already done. הלל shows the right attitude, which is trust rather than worry. The פסוק from תהלים describes exactly this kind of person.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: introduces a ברייתא
I am certain; I am confident

steps.confusionAlert: הלל is not saying he has a guarantee nothing bad happened. His confidence comes from his trust in ה׳, which is the point of the פסוק.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
An incident with Hillel the Elder
who was coming along the road
and heard a sound of screaming in the city,
he said: I am certain
that this is not in my house.
And about him the verse says:
"He shall not fear bad news;
his heart is firm, trusting in the Lord."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a story about the case of the משנה quoted in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The right response to bad news already heard is trust in ה׳, not a useless prayer

steps.title: רבא: the verse can be read in either direction
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the פסוק works read from start to end or from end to start. Either way, trust in ה׳ and not fearing bad news go together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: However you read this פסוק, from start to end or from end to start, it can be explained. From start to end: 'He shall not fear bad news.' Why? Because 'his heart is firm, trusting in ה׳.' From end to start: 'His heart is firm, trusting in ה׳,' and therefore 'he shall not fear bad news.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the פסוק that was applied to הלל. He shows it makes sense whichever half you read first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read from start to end, the second half gives the reason for the first: he does not fear because he trusts in ה׳. Read from end to start, it describes the result: a person who trusts in ה׳ will not fear bad news. Both readings teach the same lesson in different ways.

keyTerms.meaning: From its beginning to its end
From its end to its beginning

steps.whatToRemember: Trust in ה׳ is both the reason a person does not fear bad news and the sign of who he is. Like הלל, a person should respond to frightening news with trust, not with a useless prayer.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Any way that you interpret this verse
from its beginning to its end — it can be interpreted,
from its end to its beginning — it can be interpreted:
From beginning to end it is interpreted —
"He shall not fear bad news,"
what is the reason? —
"his heart is firm, trusting in the Lord."
From end to beginning it is interpreted —
"his heart is firm, trusting in the Lord,
he shall not fear bad news."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: כׇּל הֵיכִי דְּדָרְשַׁתְּ לְהַאי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the פסוק quoted about הלל in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק reads well both ways: trust in ה׳ is the cause of not fearing, and not fearing is the result of trust

steps.title: A frightened student is challenged
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי sees a frightened student and cites a verse linking fear in ציון with sinners.
steps.simpleTranslation: A student was walking behind רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי in the marketplace of ציון. When רבי ישמעאל saw that he was afraid, he said, “You are a sinner,” citing “Sinners in ציון are afraid.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about a student who looks frightened. His teacher challenges that fear with a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teacher treats the student's visible fear as a problem, not as a sign of caution. Step 28 explains which kind of fear is praised and which is a problem.

phrases.english: That student was walking
behind Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
in the marketplace of Zion.
He saw that the student was afraid.
He said to him: You are a sinner, as it is written:
“Sinners in Zion were afraid.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The story gives a concrete example of the fear and trust discussed in step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי challenges the student's fear by citing a verse.

steps.title: The student cites a verse praising fear
steps.stepSummary: The student challenges the teacher's criticism with a verse that praises a person who is always afraid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The student replied: “But is it not written, ‘Happy is the person who is always afraid’?”
steps.whatsHappening: The student brings a verse that seems to say the opposite of the teacher's verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If constant fear is praised, why was this student's fear called sinful? The two verses need to be distinguished.

phrases.english: He said to him: But is it not written,
“Happy is the person who is always afraid”!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְהָכְתִיב ״אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם מְפַחֵד תָּמִיד״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The student challenges the verse used against him.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 26 that the student's fear is blameworthy.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another verse appears to praise being afraid continually.

steps.title: The praised fear concerns Torah
steps.stepSummary: The teacher limits the student's verse to matters of תּוֹרָה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: “That verse is written about matters of תורה.”
steps.whatsHappening: The teacher answers by explaining what kind of fear the student's verse praises.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Care about one's learning is different from the fear shown in the story. The teacher therefore says the two verses address different situations.

keyTerms.meaning: that one, referring to that verse

phrases.english: He said to him: That verse
is written about matters of Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַהוּא בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The teacher narrows the meaning of the verse cited in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The two verses speak about different kinds of fear.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The student's verse praises fear in every situation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The student's verse praises fear concerning matters of תּוֹרָה.

steps.title: A sigh prompts another warning about fear
steps.stepSummary: When יהודה בר נתן sighs, רב המנונא warns him against drawing suffering upon himself and cites a verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: יהודה בר נתן was walking behind רב המנונא and sighed. רב המנונא asked whether he wanted to bring suffering upon himself, citing: “What I feared came upon me, and what I dreaded reached me.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about worry. This time, רב המנונא responds to a sigh with a warning and a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sigh is treated as an expression of dread. The cited verse connects dread with the arrival of what was feared.

phrases.aramaic: יְהוּדָה בַּר נָתָן הֲוָה שָׁקֵיל וְאָזֵיל
phrases.english: Yehuda bar Natan was walking along
behind Rav Hamnuna. He sighed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: יִסּוּרִים בָּעֵי הַהוּא גַּבְרָא
phrases.english: He said to him: Does that man want suffering
to bring upon himself? For it is written:
“For what I feared came upon me,
and what I dreaded will come to me”!

steps.triggerLanguage: יְהוּדָה בַּר נָתָן הֲוָה שָׁקֵיל וְאָזֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story tests the same distinction about fear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב המנונא warns יהודה בר נתן about his expression of dread.

steps.title: The verse praising fear is raised again
steps.stepSummary: The earlier verse about the person who fears always is brought against רב המנונא's warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is it not written, “Happy is the person who is always afraid”?
steps.whatsHappening: יהודה בר נתן answers רב המנונא with the same verse the student used in the first story, which seems to praise constant fear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב המנונא warned against dread, yet this verse seems to praise continual fear. The question asks whether his warning conflicts with that verse.

phrases.english: But is it not written:
“Happy is the person who is always afraid”!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The verse is brought as a challenge to the warning in step 29.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verse appears to praise being afraid always.

steps.title: The same distinction resolves the second story
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא answers, as רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי did, that the verse praising fear refers to matters of תּוֹרָה.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse is written about matters of תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא gives the same answer that רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי gave: the praised fear concerns תּוֹרָה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This lets the verse praise carefulness about learning without overturning רב המנונא's warning about dread. The second story confirms the distinction made in the first.

keyTerms.meaning: that one, referring to that verse

phrases.english: That verse is written about matters of Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The answer repeats the distinction established in step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limit the verse to its subject matter.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse praises dread about ordinary events.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse speaks about matters of תּוֹרָה.
steps.whatToRemember: In both stories, the answer is that “אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם מְפַחֵד תָּמִיד” concerns matters of תּוֹרָה.

steps.title: The discussion turns to entering a city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the case of entering a כְּרַךְ and introduces a teaching that asks what to say upon entry.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who enters a city. The רבנן taught: Upon entering, what does one say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the stories about fear and returns to the city-entry case. It introduces a teaching that sets up the first prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The short opening identifies the case under discussion. The question asks for the words to say when entering; the answer follows in the next step.

phrases.english: One who enters a large city.
The Sages taught: Upon entering, what does one say?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנִּכְנָס לִכְרַךְ. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בִּכְנִיסָתוֹ מַהוּ אוֹמֵר?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא changes topics from the fear stories to prayers for a city journey.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The words to say before entering a כְּרַךְ.

steps.title: Pray for a peaceful entrance
steps.stepSummary: Before entering the כְּרַךְ, a person asks ה׳ to bring him in safely.
steps.simpleTranslation: “May it be Your will, Lord my God, that You bring me into this city in peace.”
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching answers the question by giving the prayer to say before entering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a request for what has not happened yet. The later wording changes once the person has entered.

phrases.english: “May it be Your will, Lord my God,
that You bring me into this city in peace.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This supplies the prayer requested in step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Before entry, ask ה׳ to bring one into the city in peace.

steps.title: Give thanks after entering
steps.stepSummary: Once inside the כְּרַךְ, the person thanks ה׳ for a peaceful entrance.
steps.simpleTranslation: After entering, one says: “I thank You, Lord my God, that You brought me into this city in peace.”
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching moves to the moment after entry and gives a prayer of thanks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first prayer asked for safe entry. Now that entry has happened, the wording acknowledges it.

phrases.english: Once he entered, he says:
“I thank You, Lord my God,
that You brought me into this city in peace.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The request before entry becomes thanks after entry.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After entering, thank ה׳ for bringing one into the city in peace.

steps.title: Pray before leaving the city
steps.stepSummary: Before leaving the כְּרַךְ, the person asks ה׳ to bring him out safely.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he wishes to leave, he says: “May it be Your will, Lord my God and God of my ancestors, that You bring me out of this city in peace.”
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching turns from entering the city to leaving it. Before departure, it gives another request for safety.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The timing follows the same pattern as entry: ask before the event occurs. Here the requested event is a peaceful exit.

phrases.english: When he wishes to leave, he says:
“May it be Your will, Lord my God
and God of my ancestors, that You bring me out
of this city in peace.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The teaching now begins the corresponding prayers for departure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before leaving, ask ה׳ for a peaceful exit.

steps.title: Give thanks after leaving and pray for the road
steps.stepSummary: After leaving, the person thanks ה׳ for a peaceful exit and asks for protection during the journey ahead.
steps.simpleTranslation: After leaving, one thanks ה׳ for bringing him out in peace. He then asks to be led and supported in peace and protected from enemies and ambushers on the road.
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching gives the final prayer: thanks for the completed exit, followed by a request for the journey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving the city safely does not finish the journey. The prayer therefore shifts from gratitude for the exit to requests for safety on the road.

phrases.english: Once he left, he says:
“I thank You, Lord my God,
that You brought me out of this city in peace.
And just as You brought me out in peace,
so lead me in peace,
and support me in peace,
and guide my steps in peace,
and save me from the hand of every enemy
and anyone lying in ambush on the road.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The request before leaving becomes thanks after leaving, with an added request for the road.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After leaving, thank ה׳ for the safe exit and ask for protection on the journey.
steps.whatToRemember: The city prayers follow four moments: request before entry, thanks after entry, request before exit, and thanks after exit—with a prayer for the road.

steps.title: A city where people receive a trial
steps.stepSummary: רַב מַתְנָא limits the earlier prayer for entering a כְּרַךְ to a place where people may be killed without a trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב מַתְנָא says the earlier teaching applies only to a city where people are not tried before being executed. In a city where they are tried, it does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the entry prayer and gives רַב מַתְנָא’s limit on when it applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the concern is danger without a legal process. Where a trial takes place, רַב מַתְנָא says that concern does not call for this prayer.

phrases.english: Rav Mattana said:
They taught this only about a city
where people are not tried and executed,
but in a city where people are tried and executed
— it does not apply.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מַתְנָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the earlier prayer on entering a city after the sequence of entry and exit prayers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, the entry prayer applies to a city where people may be killed without being tried, but not to a city that tries people first.

steps.title: Another version includes a city with trials
steps.stepSummary: A second version of רַב מַתְנָא says the prayer matters even where people receive a trial.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רַב מַתְנָא said: Even in a city where people are tried and executed, a person might not find someone to argue in his favor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a different version of רַב מַתְנָא’s statement. This version keeps the prayer relevant even when the city holds trials.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A trial does not guarantee that someone will speak up for the person. That remaining risk explains why this version does not remove the need for prayer.

phrases.english: Some say that Rav Mattana said:
Even in a city where people are tried and executed,
sometimes there may not be available to him
a person who argues in his favor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different version of the same sage’s ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even where trials take place, the entry prayer remains relevant because no one may present a defense.

steps.title: A prayer before entering the bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: A teaching gives a prayer asking for safety in the bathhouse and saying that, if death occurs, it should bring atonement.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Before entering the bathhouse, a person asks ה׳ to save him from harm there and from similar harm. He asks that no ruin or wrongdoing happen to him; if it does, he asks that his death atone for all his sins.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new case: what to say before entering a bathhouse. It quotes the full proposed prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prayer begins by asking for protection. Its final sentence raises the possibility of death, which is the wording אַבָּיֵי will address next.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One who enters a bathhouse
says: “May it be Your will
Lord my God, that You save me from this
and from similar things, and do not let happen to me
any harm or wrongdoing.
And if there does happen to me
any harm or wrongdoing
— may my death be atonement
for all my sins.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the city-entry prayer to a new prayer for entering a bathhouse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The quoted teaching directs a person entering a bathhouse to pray for safety and includes a request about atonement if death occurs.

steps.title: Do not say the prayer that way
steps.stepSummary: אַבָּיֵי objects to the prayer’s wording because a person should not speak of possible disaster in that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: אַבָּיֵי said: A person should not say it that way, so as not to open his mouth to Satan.
steps.whatsHappening: אַבָּיֵי rejects saying the bathhouse prayer exactly as quoted. His concern is its mention of a bad outcome happening to the speaker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier teaching includes the words “if harm happens to me” and asks about the speaker’s death. אַבָּיֵי says not to introduce that possibility in one’s own prayer.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage objecting to the wording
to Satan; part of the warning against speaking of misfortune

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לָא לֵימָא אִינָשׁ הָכִי,
phrases.english: Abaye said: A person should not say it this way,
so as not to open his mouth to Satan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לָא לֵימָא אִינָשׁ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to wording in the prayer just quoted.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The bathhouse prayer’s wording about possible harm and death, not the practice of asking for protection.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It has the speaker raise a possible bad outcome.

steps.title: Support for avoiding talk of misfortune
steps.stepSummary: A teaching attributed to רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ and רַבִּי יוֹסֵי supports אַבָּיֵי’s warning.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ said, and it was also taught in the name of רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: A person should never open his mouth to the שטן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now supports אַבָּיֵי’s objection with a broader warning from earlier sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אַבָּיֵי’s objection is not limited to this one prayer. The quoted rule says generally not to bring up possible misfortune in one’s own words.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage in whose name it was taught: the תנא רבי יוסי (see the note)
always or never, depending on the sentence

steps.whatToRemember: The bathhouse prayer asks for safety, but אַבָּיֵי objects to its wording about possible harm and death.

phrases.english: For Reish Lakish said,
and it was likewise taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
phrases.notes: The printed text here reads רב יוסי, but וכן תנא marks a teaching of a תנא, so it is the תנא רבי יוסי, as Sefaria translates it and as the same saying reads on ברכות י״ט ע״א and כתובות ח׳ ע״ב.

phrases.english: A person should never open
his mouth to Satan.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, וְכֵן תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב יוֹסֵי:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies an earlier teaching that supports אַבָּיֵי’s objection.
steps.raayaObject: אַבָּיֵי’s warning not to say the prayer in a way that raises possible misfortune.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The warning stated by רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ and taught in the name of רַבִּי יוֹסֵי.

steps.title: A verse supports the warning about speech
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף points to verses in which a comparison to סדום is followed by the prophet addressing the people as leaders of סדום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף asks which verse illustrates the warning. One verse says, “We were almost like סדום”; the prophet’s reply then calls them “leaders of סדום.”
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף brings a verse to support the warning from the previous step. He draws attention to how the prophet’s wording follows the people’s earlier comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse says they were *almost* like סדום. The next verse addresses them as leaders of סדום, making that earlier wording sound troubling.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: What is the verse?
As it is written: “We were almost like Sodom,

phrases.aramaic: לַעֲמֹרָה דָּמִינוּ״, מַאי אַהְדַּר לְהוּ נָבִיא —
phrases.english: we resembled Gomorrah.” What did the prophet reply to them?
“Hear the word of the Lord, leaders of Sodom,” and so forth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a verse illustrating the warning cited in step 41.
steps.raayaObject: The warning against speaking of possible disaster.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The successive verses comparing the people to סדום and then addressing them as leaders of סדום.

steps.title: What does a person say on leaving the bathhouse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the bathhouse and asks what a person says after coming out.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a person comes out, what does he say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the bathhouse discussion and sets up the next prayer. It asks about the moment of leaving, rather than entering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion concerned what to say before entering the bathhouse. Now the focus shifts to what to say after emerging safely.

phrases.english: When he comes out, what does he say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the verse about careful speech and returns to the bathhouse prayer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The words to say upon leaving the bathhouse.

steps.title: Thank God after leaving the bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא gives a short prayer of thanks for being saved from the fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא said: “I thank You, Lord, for saving me from the fire.”
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא answers the question with the words to say on leaving. The person thanks God for having come out safely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a prayer after the danger has passed. Its focus is gratitude for safety, not a prediction that harm will occur.

phrases.english: Rav Aḥa said:
“I give thanks before You, Lord,
for You saved me from the fire.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers what to say after leaving the bathhouse.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Thank God for being saved from the fire.

steps.title: A bathhouse collapse shows why thanks matters
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו survives a bathhouse collapse, saves others, and recognizes the force of רב אחא’s prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו entered a bathhouse. Its floor collapsed beneath him, but a miracle let him stand on a pillar and save one hundred and one men with one arm. He said, “This is what רב אחא meant.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that makes the bathhouse danger concrete. After surviving and saving others, רבי אבהו connects his experience to רב אחא’s words of thanks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The collapse shows why leaving a bathhouse safely could call for gratitude. רבי אבהו’s closing words point back to the prayer in the previous step.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu entered a bathhouse.
The bathhouse collapsed beneath him,

phrases.aramaic: אִתְרְחִישׁ לֵיהּ נִיסָּא קָם עַל עַמּוּדָא,
phrases.english: a miracle happened for him, and he stood on a pillar;
he saved one hundred and one men
with one of his limbs.
He said: This is what Rav Aḥa meant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the danger behind רב אחא’s prayer of thanks.
steps.raayaObject: The relevance of thanking God for safety after leaving the bathhouse.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אבהו’s experience of the bathhouse collapse.

steps.title: A prayer before bloodletting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces another statement by רב אחא: before bloodletting, a person asks God for healing and acknowledges God as the true healer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא said that a person entering for bloodletting asks God to make the procedure healing and to heal him. He calls God a faithful healer, then says that healing is not naturally in human hands, though people have made a practice of treating others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to another risky activity and gives רב אחא’s prayer before bloodletting. This sets up a new discussion about human treatment and God’s healing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person asks that this particular procedure help rather than harm. The prayer credits God with healing, while its final line raises a question about the role of human healers.

keyTerms.meaning: that they have made it a practice

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב אַחָא: הַנִּכְנָס לְהַקִּיז דָּם,
phrases.english: As Rav Aḥa said: One who enters to let blood
says: “May it be Your will, Lord my God,
that this undertaking be for my healing,

phrases.aramaic: וּתְרַפְּאֵנִי. כִּי אֵל רוֹפֵא נֶאֱמָן אָתָּה
phrases.english: and heal me. For You are a faithful healing God,
and Your healing is true, because it is not their way

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם לְרַפּאוֹת אֶלָּא שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ״.
phrases.english: for human beings to heal, but they have made it a practice.”

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב אַחָא: הַנִּכְנָס לְהַקִּיז דָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the bathhouse story to another statement attributed to רב אחא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before bloodletting, ask God to make the procedure healing and to heal the patient.

steps.title: Doctors have permission to heal
steps.stepSummary: אביי says not to use the wording just introduced, because a teaching from רבי ישמעאל says Scripture permits doctors to heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: A person should not say it that way. The school of רבי ישמעאל taught that “and he shall surely heal” teaches that a doctor has been given permission to heal.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges the wording of the prayer before bloodletting. He brings a teaching from רבי ישמעאל to show that seeking a doctor's help is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous prayer stressed that God is the true healer. אביי's concern is wording that could make a doctor's work sound improper; the verse explicitly gives doctors permission to heal.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לָא לֵימָא אִינָשׁ הָכִי,
phrases.english: Abaye said: A person should not say it this way,
for the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
“And he shall surely heal”—from here we learn that permission was given
to a doctor to heal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לָא לֵימָא אִינָשׁ הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אביי challenges the wording of רב אחא's prayer before bloodletting.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the prayer before bloodletting in step 46.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verse grants doctors permission to heal, so the prayer should not speak as though their work is improper.

steps.title: What does one say afterward?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what a person says upon standing up after bloodletting.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a person stands up, what does he say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the prayer before bloodletting to a new question about what to say afterward. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion concerned words said before the procedure. The question now asks for words to say once it is over.

phrases.english: When he stands up, what does he say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא turns from what to say before bloodletting to what to say afterward.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The words to say after bloodletting.

steps.title: A blessing after bloodletting
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא gives a short blessing that praises God as the healer who charges nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא said: “Blessed … who heals without payment.”
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא answers the question with the words to say after bloodletting. The blessing thanks God for healing without payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is an after-the-procedure blessing, not a replacement for the prayer discussed earlier. The quoted source leaves out words in the middle of the blessing.
steps.whatToRemember: Before bloodletting, the wording must respect the permission given to doctors. Afterward, רב אחא says a blessing of thanks.

phrases.english: Rav Aḥa said: “Blessed … who heals without payment.”
phrases.notes: The ellipsis appears in the text here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב אחא supplies the words requested by the question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Say a blessing praising God as רוֹפֵא חִנָּם.
